source.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning

record.file_problem: none; the complete paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests toy-model superposition geometry using the toy autoencoder setup, with feature-group structure and mutual exclusiveness as the focus; it also argues that mutual exclusiveness is more fundamental than overall sparsity.
record.gate_note: The paper reports toy-model feature geometry, reconstruction error, and results across group sparsity, feature-group structure, and dimensionality. The GPT-2 and larger-model experiments concern whether NDM-derived subspaces align with circuit variables or knowledge-routing effects, not whether sparse features overlap in the sense of the listed versions. The SAE-clustering comparison evaluates that subspace method on circuit tests; it does not test SAE features as complete or canonical model units. NDM's own partitioning results are not included as rows because they evaluate the method's recovery of subspaces rather than the toy model's superposition geometry.
record.test_reason: Mainly a methods paper, but Sec. 2 and App. C.1 train Elhage-style toy autoencoders (z > d) with grouped, mutually exclusive features and report W^T W geometry. The authors argue explicitly that mutual exclusiveness, not uniform sparsity, is the more fundamental condition for superposition. That restates the condition V1 gives, so T5 rather than T2. The GPT-2, Qwen and Gemma parts evaluate NDM's own subspaces, not superposition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record overweights the toy results. The authors' main conclusion is that NDM, an unsupervised neighbor-distance objective with MI-based merging, decomposes representation space into interpretable, relatively independent, non-basis-aligned subspaces. These subspaces align with GPT-2 circuit variables (average Gini 0.71, above baselines) and separate knowledge-routing mechanisms in 2B models. The toy results serve as motivation: mutually exclusive feature groups superpose within orthogonal subspaces, and mutual exclusiveness may be more fundamental than sparsity.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Elhage et al. toy autoencoder formulation, but emphasizes grouped feature dependencies and mutual exclusiveness rather than only uniform feature sparsity; it also introduces NDM for finding subspaces in real models.
record.method_sensitivity: Toy-model geometry varies with group sparsity, feature-group frequency, and hidden dimensionality. The paper reports weaker cross-group orthogonality at higher group sparsity and superposition of lower-frequency groups when dimensions are insufficient.

fits_no_version.finding: NDM finds multi-dimensional subspaces in GPT-2 Small whose patching effects concentrate on circuit variables. Average Gini is 0.71, versus 0.56 for SAE-feature-cluster subspaces and 0.21–0.38 for identity, random and PCA baselines. Qualitatively, the subspaces encode current token, previous token, position and topic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM residual streams decompose into roughly independent multi-dimensional subspaces acting as variables (feature groups). This bears on multi-dimensional feature structure, but it measures the method's own performance.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5-1.5B and Gemma-2-2B, separate NDM subspaces mediate parametric versus context knowledge routing under subspace patching.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distinct knowledge-routing mechanisms are mediated by separable residual-stream subspaces.

record.problems: Toy-model coverage is limited: the authors note they did not extensively vary feature-group count, unit size, or search number. Some tested low-dimensional configurations have poor reconstruction, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the toy results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional toy-model result bearing on the listed versions was left out. GPT-2 and larger-model subspace-patching outcomes and SAE-clustering comparisons are omitted because they test NDM's alignment with circuit variables or knowledge-routing effects, not the claim versions' feature-overlap, neuron-capacity, or canonical-SAE-unit measures.

untested.parts: Phase transition across uniform per-feature sparsity, the effect of feature-importance weighting, and regular polytope geometry. Only group sparsity at S = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 is varied, and all features have equal importance.
Neuron-level polysemanticity and dedicated dimensions for important features are not examined.
The LLM experiments measure NDM subspace patching concentration, not feature spread across neurons or SAE recovery.
SAE-cluster subspaces are used only as a baseline; there is no test of completeness, stability or canonicity.
No test of whether naturally learned features are 1-D or multi-dimensional; toy feature groups are imposed by the data generator.

record.verdict_notes: Toy-model results come from figures and text only, with no numeric orthogonality measure and no uncertainty estimates. The FVU rows are not superposition measures. V6 links were dropped because multi-dimensional group structure is imposed by the data generator rather than tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests toy models with specific feature-group distributions and dimensionalities; it does not establish a general transition across arbitrary sparsity levels or feature-importance distributions.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated neuron dimensions while less important features share them.
Does not investigate polysemantic neurons arising for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The language-model experiments examine learned subspaces, not feature spread across neurons or recovery of sparse features with an SAE.
Discusses differences between SAE features and subspaces, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.
Provides toy-model evidence and an interpretation of feature groups as multidimensional units, but does not establish that all forms of superposition in trained models have this geometry.

rows.note: The authors describe small interference between almost-orthogonal features and orthogonal subspaces for the two groups.

rows.measure: Cross-group orthogonality in W^T W; the paper reports that orthogonality is weaker at higher group sparsity.
rows.value: Figure 7c; cross-group blocks are nonzero, though their absolute values are smaller.
rows.note: The authors interpret higher group sparsity as making groups less likely to co-occur and encouraging superposition; the reported cross-group orthogonality is nevertheless weaker.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. Nonzero cross-group products at S=0.75 mean more superposition as co-occurrence drops. That is the sparsity-dependent direction V1 predicts, and the authors read it this way.

rows.size_stated: z = 40, d = 10; groups of 5, 15, 5, and 15 features
rows.operation_detail: Inspect feature-direction geometry under four feature groups and limited hidden dimensionality.
rows.measure: Feature-group geometry and reconstruction: there is not enough dimension to allocate an orthogonal subspace to each group; features from the second and fourth groups are superposed, and reconstruction is poor.
rows.value: The second and fourth groups are superposed; FVU = 0.166.
rows.note: The authors say the second and fourth groups have lower frequency than the other two.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. Under a capacity limit (d=10), the lower-frequency groups are superposed while the others keep orthogonal subspaces, as V1 expects. The poor FVU (0.166) is a consequence, not a failure of the effect. V6 link removed.

relationships.condition: Toy ReLU autoencoders, z > d, grouped mutually exclusive features, equal importance
relationships.reason: Same-group features are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions (r1, r10–r13). Cross-group superposition appears as group sparsity rises (r3, r5, r7). Lower-frequency groups are superposed when dimensions are scarce (r9), and superposition recedes when d grows (r11).
relationships.display_finding: Features within a group were stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, and superposition across groups appeared as group sparsity rose. Lower-frequency groups were superposed when dimensions were scarce, and superposition receded as d grew.

relationships.display_finding: Superposition stayed within mutually exclusive groups, and co-occurring groups sat in orthogonal subspaces. The authors argue that mutual exclusiveness, not sparsity per se, is the condition.
